utterances: M: How you doing?
F: Okay.
F: Yeah. Wow.
M: We're all going to miss him.
F: Mmm hmm. I never knew it was going to be this hard, you know.
F: It's weird 'cause it's like you expected it to happen and eventually-
F: he had cancer, you know?
F: They thought he got--would get better and he did, and then it just- things turned bad.
F: Turned around for the worst, you know.
M: I didn't know him, Tricia, but uh- I heard that he was a great man.
F: He was amazing.
F: I loved that boy.
F: We did everything together, you know.
F: It's weird, I think. I feel so alone, you know? What am I going to do now? Now that he's gone.
F: He's so young. It seems so--
F: so wrong in so many ways.
F: His poor parents. You know, it's their only son.
M: yeah.
F: Kind of a whole year. I mean, he suffered with this, this monster, this thing, this disease.
M: He was in chemo the whole time, right?
M: And he just got that baseball scholarship.
F: I know. He was, he had so much going for him.
F: So handsome, so young, so gifted.
F: So talented.
F: Such a sweet person, you know?
M: How's his parents doing?
F: Not very good.
F: Can you imagine, though, you know, as a parent, just losing a kid? Twenty-two years old.
F: It's weird, I kind of feel like part of me is gone now, you know?
F: Because this other half was just kind of like ripped away.
M: You guys were pretty close, weren't you?
F: He was like, he was like my brother, you know.
F: He was my brother.
F: Just seems so unfair, is the way it is.
F: You know, he had that really pretty girlfriend for like about a year and-
M: What was her name?
F: Kelly. Kelly Uveny.
F: They talked about getting married and--
M: Trying to have a baby.
F: Yeah. But then when he got cancer and it got bad, you know, she just took off and-
F: so I was there for him.
M: Some people.
M: Yeah, but you were there all the hospital days. By his bed-
F: Yeah. God, I loved that kid.
M: So nice, so positive.
F: yeah.
M: We need more people like him.
F: Joe, do you think he knew I loved him?
M: I don't know.
F: I never told him, I love you, but-
F: I loved him so much.
M: I don't know if Benny was smart like that- but-
M: I'm sure he loved you too. He just didn't know it.

F: You know, it's lovely here, the air is sweet.
F: No, not sorry.  But, um. But I'm not gonna stay.
M: The trouble is, I planned on sort of sneaking up on you on a period of a week or so.  But they take it for granted that we're all set.
F: I knew they would, your mother anyway.
F: Well, from her point of view, why else would I come?
F: I guess this is why I came.
M: I'm embarrassing you and I didn't want to tell it to you here.  I wanted some place we'd never been before.  A place where we'd be brand new to each other.
F: Well, you started to write me
M: You felt something that far back?
F: Every day since.
M: Ann, why didn't you let me know?
M: Let's drive someplace.  I want to be alone with you.
M: No.  Nothing like that.
F: Well, what's wrong?  I mean, even in your letters there was some--something ashamed.
M: Yeah, I suppose I have been.  But it's going from me.
F: It wouldn't work this way.
M: Well, I lost them.
M: Just about all.
M: It takes some time for a guy to toss that off.  'Cause they weren't just men.

M: For instance, this one time, it had been raining several days and this kid came to me and gave me his last pair of dry socks.  I put them in pocket.  It's only a little thing, but those are the kind of guys I had.
M: They didn't die, they killed themselves for each other.  I mean that exactly.  I mean, a little more selfish and they'd have been here today.
M: I got this idea watching 'em go down.  Everything was being destroyed, see, but it seemed that one new thing was made.  A sort of responsibility.  Man for man. You know what I mean?
M: To show that, to bring that onto the Earth again, like some kind of monument and everyone can feel it standing behind him and it would make a difference to him.
M: Then I came back and it was incredible.  There was no meaning in it here. I mean, the whole thing to them seemed like it's sort of a bus accident.  I went to work with Dad and that rat race again.

M: And I felt what you said, ashamed somehow 'cause nobody had changed at all.  It seemed to make suckers out of a lot of guys.  I felt wrong to be alive to open the new bank book, drive the new car, see the new refrigerator.

M: I mean, you can take those things out of a war, but when you drive that car, you've gotta realize that it came out of the love a man can have for a man.  You've gotta be a little better because of it.
M: Otherwise all you have is really loot and there's blood on it.  And I didn't want to take any of that.  And I guess that included you.
F: Do you still feel that way?
M: I want you now Annie.
F: 'Cause you mustn't feel that way.  Because you have a right to everything you have, Chris.  Everything, you understand that?  Me too.
F: I mean, and your money, there's- there's nothing wrong with your money.  I mean, your father put hundreds of planes in the air.  A man should be paid for that.
F: What'll I do with a fortune?

M: I don't care then.
M: Hello?  Hello?  What?  Wrong number.
F: Ah, it send shivers up my spine.
F: Behave exquisitely.
M: With the most perfect poise?
F: Oh, of course.  I shall probably do a court curtsy.
M: Things that ought to matter dreadfully don't matter at all when one's happy.  Do they?
F: What's so horrible is that one can't stay happy.
M: Oh, darling, don't say that.
F: It's true.  The whole business is a very poor joke.
M: Meaning that sacred and beautiful thing, love?
F: Yes, meaning just that.
M: You mustn't be serious, my dear one.  That's just what they want.
F: Who's they?
M: All those futile moralists that try to make life unbearable.  Laugh at them.  Be flippant.  Laugh at everything.  All their sacred shibboleths.
M: Flippancy brings out the acid in their damn sweetness and light.
F: If I laugh at everything, then I must laugh at us too.
M: Certainly, you must.  We're figures of fun, alright.
F: Well how long will it last us, this ludicrous overbearing love of ours.
M: Who knows.
F: Well, shall we always want to bicker and fight?
M: No, that desire will fade.  Along with our passion.
F: Oh, dear, shall we like that?
M: Depends on how well we've played.
F: Well, what happens if one of us dies?  I mean, does the one that's left still laugh?
M: Yes.  Yes. With all his might.
M: No. No, it isn't.  Death is very laughable.  Such a cunning little mystery.  All done with mirrors.
F: Darling, I believe you're talking nonsense.
M: So is everyone else in the long run.

F: Oh, thank you, dear.  The same applies to you except that if I catch so much as looking at another woman, I'll kill you.
M: You remember that awful scene we had in Venice?

F: Charles.  That was his name.  Charles.  He did wriggle so beautifully.

M: How long did that row last?

F: It burned my comb too and all the towels in the bathroom.
F: That was the first time you ever hit me.
M: I didn't hit you very hard.
F: The manager came in and found us rolling around on the floor, biting and scratching like panthers.
M: Oh, I'll never forget his face.

M: Carla, can I ask you something?  Don't take this wrong, but are you having your period?
F: God damn it, Augie, don't ask me that.  I hate it when you ask me that.  You always ask me that.  It's insulting.
M: Well, what's bugging you?
F: We just have different ideas of what this evening is supposed to look like.
M: There's nothing to it.  We come here, the grunion arrive, they do their little fish business, we go ooh, ah, look at the fish.  They go home. We go home.
F: For heaven sake, we're not going to see the grunions.
M: Why not?
F: We never do, do we?  I mean, have we ever?
M: We've missed them twice.  That's not ever.
F: Twice is every time we've tried. That's ever.
M: Well, we'll see them this year.
F: No, we won't.  It's pointless.  It's like waiting up to see Santa Claus.
F: I mean, I feel like my whole life is gonna be spent standing on the beach with my eyes wide open and my hands clasped expectantly waiting for the fish to show up.  And the fish won't show up.
M: I thought you wanted to see it.
F: You don't understand anything I'm saying.
M: No, of course not.
F: I did want to see it.  I always do.  I keep thinking that this is gonna be the time and it never is.
M: It's just fish.  Nothing to get traumatized about.
M: All right.  Look, I've been trying to work this backwards, but I cannot seem to figure out the exact moment that we took a turn for the worst.
M: You said, "Hey the grunion are running tonight."  I said, "Great, let's go.  I feel lucky."
M: Okay, so I'm putting on my jacket, putting out the animals, getting the car out of the garage--
F: Do you remember the first time we came to see it?  It was about four years ago, right after we got married.
F: I thought I was pregnant, you had a bottle of champagne, but no glasses.  You asked me to dance, so we kicked off our shoes and you popped the cork.
F: And while we were dancing, you said the softest, most intimate things to me right into my ear so that I could feel them as much as hear them.
F: And I remember thinking, this is it.  You know, at last--at last I am as happy as I am supposed to be.
M: Wait a minute.  I've got it.
F: Just dancing barefoot in the sand, drinking champagne out of the bottle.
M: It was in the car, right?  Driving past the Knickerbocker Liquor Locker, you said, "let's get some champagne," and I said, "time's a wasting" or something like that, right?
M: Yeah, of course, I see it now.  You want this to be like that other time, right?  That's it, right?
F: I'd rather not remember some things.  I would rather not hope for some things.
M: Okay, yeah, sure, I see it now.  Listen, you wanna dance?
F: No.
M: You want me to go get some champagne?
F: No.
M: Take off our shoes?
M: Well, what?  You want me to breathe in your ear?
F: No.
M: You wanna get married again?
F: No.
M: What?  What?  You want a divorce?
F: No.
M: A vacation?
F: No.
M: A new carpet?  A poodle?  Ice cream?  Back rub?  A suicide pact?  What?  What?  Carla, what the hell do you want?
M: Well, welcome to the human race.  Do you think this is what I had in mind when I proposed?  That four years down the road, we'd be at the beach yelling at each other over fish?

M: No, Carla, I'm just like you.  I thought it was gonna be all peaches and roses and sand in our toes and wind in our hair and the fish will always come and the bills will pay themselves and we'll have three fat rosy kids and ha, ha, baby, the joke's on us
M: 'cause you know what you get, Carla?  You know what you get?  This.
M: Yes, it is.
M: Right.
F: Well.  This isn't anything like I thought anything would be like.
M: I know, me neither.
M: I'm doing the best I can.
F: I know that, Augie.  Really, I do.
F: I know that you meant this to be special and nice and the sand and the moon and all, but I just couldn't help thinking about being somewhere else.
M: Maybe if you were with somebody else too.
F: I didn't say that.
M: No, I know.  But still.  I know I don't make you happy.
F: You're the one who probably wishes you were with someone else.  Someone who--you'd rather enjoy yourself and didn't take everything so hard.
M: I don't know.  It seemed like a pretty good spot to me.  I mean, look at the view you have of the moon from here.
M: Well, look what we have here.
F: Augie, you brought refreshments.
M: It's not champagne.
F: Well, then we don't need glasses.
F: No.  I think you might be right.  Maybe this is the spot after all.
F: Augie, I'm sorry.
M: Shh.  If we're very quiet the fish might come.
F: Or not.
M: Or not.

F: I almost got married two years ago.
F: You started to write me and--
F: Every day since.
F: I will never forgive you.  Why did you wait all these years?  All I did was sit and wonder if I was crazy for thinking of you.
M: No.  Nothing like that.
F: Then, what's wrong?  I mean, even in your letters there was some--something ashamed.
M: Yeah, I suppose I have been.  But it's going from me.
F: You've gotta tell me.
M: I don't know how to start.
F: It wouldn't work this way.
M: It's all mixed up with so many other things.  You remember overseas, I was in command of a company?
F: Yeah, sure.
M: Well, I lost them.
F: How many?
M: Just about all.
F: Oh, gee.
M: It takes some time for a guy to toss that off.  'Cause they weren't just men.

M: For instance, one time, it had been raining several days and this kid came to me and gave me his last pair of dry socks.  I put them in pocket.  It's only a little thing, but that's the kind of guys I had.
M: They didn't die, they killed themselves for each other.  I mean that exactly.  A little more selfish and they'd have been here today.
M: I got this idea watching them go down.  Everything was being destroyed, see, but it seemed that there was one new thing being made.  A sort of responsibility.  Man for man.

M: Then I came back and it was incredible.  There was no meaning in it here.  The whole thing to them seemed like sort of a bus accident.  I went to work with Dad and that rat race again.

M: And I felt what you said, ashamed somehow 'cause nobody was changed at all.  It seemed to make suckers out of a lot of guys.  I felt wrong to be alive to open the new bank book, drive the new car, see the new refrigerator.

M: I mean, you can take those things out of a war, but when you drive that car, you've gotta know that it came out of the love a man can have for a man.  You've gotta be a little better because of it.
M: Because otherwise all you have is really loot and there's blood on it.  And I didn't want to take any of it.  And I guess that included you.
F: You still feel that way?

M: This is really-this is unfair.
F: I know.
M: I don't see [BREATHING]
F: I don't know what to say.  I don't want to go but I don't have a lot of choice.
M: I mean we both knew that this was going to happen.  It's just that I feel that, you know, I don't want Susie growing up without a mother.
M: And, uh, I'm afraid that if you, you know, when you leave, you won't come back.
F: I'm going to come back.  I need you to believe that.
M: You don't know that.
M: I'll believe it, but- I'll believe it but it- I don't know that that's going to happen.
F: Well you have to have faith because I don't have a choice and I have to go.
F: Do you think I want to leave you?
M: You have a choice.
F: I have to do this.  I don't want to leave.  Do you think I want to miss seeing her grow up?
M: I know.  It's just you don't have to do this for a living you know.
M: You're a smart person.  There are other things you can do.
F: Look we both knew what this meant when I signed on
F: And now- and now it's really shitty timing but now I have to go.
F: I mean I'm the one who has to leave here.  I'm the one who has to leave the two of you.  At least you get to be together.
F: What's that supposed to mean?
M: I mean we can't-we're not a complete family without you here.
F: Well I'll come back.  What is that supposed to mean?  You're not willing to wait for me to come back?

M: Of course I'm going to wait.  I just- I just don't like the idea of this happening because this isn't the last time this is going to happen. You're going to go on more tours and stuff.  I just- I can't-
M: I can't deal with this emotionally.
F: What do you want me to do?
M: I want you to leave.  I want you to leave the service.
F: Well I can't very well do it today.  I still have to leave tomorrow.
M: You can do it today.  You don't have to do anything.  You don't have to do anything you don't want to do.
F: You're not making this any easier for me, you know.  I'm the one who has to go and you're really not helping.
M: Look I'm just telling you that you don't have to go.
F: I do have to go. And I need to know that you're here waiting for me and that you believe that I'm coming back.
M: That's all I'm saying... No you don't.
F: Thanks that helps.
M: It's just really unfair.  This is- this is bullshit.
F: I feel much better now.
M: You're acting like, you know, you're the one who's going all through, you know, all this shit and it's really- it's really not.
F: I know I'm leaving you here with all the responsibility but at least you get to be with her.
M: Yeah.  Of course I do because I didn't enlist in this stupid thing.  Why don't you just get out now and then-
F: I will but I can't right now.
M: Then go.  We'll be here when you get back.
F: That's how you want to leave it?
M: I don't know how else to leave it.  What, do you want me to lie to you?
M: You want me tell you that I'm okay with it?
F: I want you to be okay with it as much as you can be.  I mean it's not a great situation but we don't have an option here.
M: Well I can't be okay with it the same way you can't not go.  It just doesn't work that way.
F: Fine.

utterances: M: You're not sorry you came?
F: No.  I'm not sorry.  But I'm not going to stay.
F: Look,
F: you saw the way that she acted and then well, I mean, you, you were acting kind of...
M: What?
F: Well, I don't know, embarrassed of her since I came.
M: I mean, that's the reason why I asked you here.
F: Well,
M: I love you.
F: I guess that's why I came.
F: Look, I've been ready for a long, long time now.
F: Look, I almost got married two years ago.
F: You started to write me.
M: You felt something that far back.
F: Every day since.
F: I was waiting for you Chris, I mean, till then you never wrote and then when you did what did you say?
F: You'd always be so ambiguous.
M: Give me a kiss Ann, just give me...
M: Oh God.  Annie, I kissed Annie.  I kissed Annie.
F: I'll never forgive you for that.
F: I mean,  Why did you wait all these years?  There I was sitting around and wondering if I was crazy for thinking about you.
M: We're going to live now.  I'm going to make you so happy.
F: Not like that you're not.
M: Nothing.  Hey, let's drive somewhere.  I want to be alone with you.
M: You remember overseas I was in command of a company?
M: Well I lost them.
F: How many?
M: Just about all.
F: Geez.
M: Takes a little while to toss that off cause they weren't just men.
M: For instance, one time this...it had been raining several days and this one kid, he came up to me, he gave me his last pair of dry socks, put them in my pocket.
M: That's just a little thing but that's the kind of guys I had.  They didn't just die, they killed themselves for each other and I mean that exactly.
M: A little more selfish and they'd still be here today.  And I got this idea watching them go down.  See everything was being destroyed but there was one new thing that was being created.
M: It was a kind of responsibility, man for man.  You understand me?
M: And to show that and to bring that onto the earth again like some sort of monument standing right behind all of us and we could feel it and it would make a difference to him.
M: And then I came here and it was incredible.  There was no meaning in it here.  The whole thing to them was a kind of bus accident.
M: And I went to work with dad and that rat race again and I felt what you said, ashamed.  Somehow because nobody was changed at all.
M: It seemed to make a sucker out of a lot of guys.  I felt wrong to be alive.  I felt wrong to have that new checkbook,
M: open that new bank account, drive the new car and see the new refrigerator

M: cause you can take those things out of the war.  But you got to know, when you drive that car that it came out of the love that a man can have for a man and you got to be a little bit better because of that.
M: Otherwise what you have is loot and there's blood on it.
M: And I didn't want to take any of it and I guess that included you.
F: And you still feel that way?

F: that includes me too, I mean and the money, you have right to that money.  Your father put planes up in the air, good planes and he deserves it, you should be proud of that.  A man should be paid for that.
M: Annie I'm going to make a fortune for you.
F: What am I going to do with a fortune?
M: Buy some hats?
